title: Four channels, one denominator
task: Find out what the agreeing numbers were computed from
scene: Four of Halden's five numbers agree to within a few percent. The fifth, a mechanical gauge nobody has touched in a year, does not. Merrick has the derivation sheets and is waiting.
question: Everything except the mechanical gauge agrees. Open the derivations, keep what still stands, and name the source at fault.
takeaway: Independence is a property of the measurement chain, not of how many displays report it.
why: Three of these numbers are ratios, and a ratio is a comparison: it carries the error of whatever sits underneath the line. The vault was assumed to be rock and is not, so every quantity divided by it is wrong by the same factor and they agree with each other beautifully while doing it. That is what makes a common-mode error survive review — nothing looks inconsistent. The correction is arithmetic on exactly those three and nothing else: the gauge measured a pressure directly and the counts came off a separate network, so neither of them ever touched the bad denominator and neither should move.
assumes: a ratio inherits the error of whatever it was divided by
two displays fed from one sensor are one measurement
answerText: The old vault. It was treated as a competent-rock reference and reads 1.6 times rock in the working band, so every ratio computed against it is low by that factor — and the mechanical gauge and the event counts, which never used it, keep their evidence.

title: What the level rise leaves out
task: Account for the whole flow, not the part that shows
scene: The bilge is up eight centimetres in a minute over four square metres of deck. The drain pump has been running the whole time. Tomas Oyelaran wants the leak rate, not the rise.
question: Read what you need and report the total inflow at the hull.
takeaway: An accumulation rate is the inflow minus everything already being removed from it.
why: The level in the bilge is not the leak; it is what got past the pump. Anything already being removed while you were measuring has to go back into the total, and a pump that has been running since the alarm is easy to leave out precisely because it is not a reading — nothing on the panel changes when it runs. Report the 320 and the response is sized for a leak two thirds of its actual rate, which decides how many pumps are worth starting and, more to the point, whether starting pumps is the answer at all.
assumes: a volume rate is a level rate multiplied by a plan area
what accumulates is what is left after everything already leaving has left
answerText: About 410 litres a minute — the 320 that accumulated plus the 90 the pump had already discharged during the same minute.

title: The signature and the thing it stands for
task: Close the list on evidence rather than on signatures
scene: The closing checklist is signed throughout. Naidoo has the watch bill open beside it and has not said anything yet. There is time to verify three items.
question: Verify what the time allows and hold whatever cannot be closed on the evidence present.
takeaway: A record is evidence that somebody accepted a claim, which is not evidence for the claim.
why: A checklist is a compression of experience, and its signatures record who accepted each claim at the time. That is worth having and it is not the same as the condition being true now. The two items that fail here fail differently: one was signed for a space nobody could enter, and one is contradicted by a direct measurement at the boundary, which beats a written record every time because it is the actual state rather than the reported one. Verifying the whole list is not available, so the decision that matters is which claims would hurt if they were wrong.
assumes: a signature records responsibility, not a physical condition
an indication reports a commanded state rather than a measured one
answerText: Hold the aft escape route and breaker 2B. Both are critical, both were signed, and neither has evidence that supports the claim — the route is obstructed and the conductor is live whatever the log says.

title: One slot, three good proposals
task: Buy the thing that would change the decision
scene: Three proposals, one funded slot, and a crew that mobilises at noon either way. Calderón has read all three and will not say which she prefers.
question: You have four hours of the day's budget. Buy what changes what the crew does at noon.
takeaway: A measurement earns its cost by changing a decision that has not yet been taken.
why: Two of these proposals measure the surface again. They are careful and they will produce a tighter number about a place nobody is standing, which is the failure this decision exists to avoid: a measurement can be rigorous and still answer a question whose answer does not enter the choice. The test that separates them is whether a result the other way changes anything, and only the gallery reading does — a low oxygen four metres down stops the entry, while a third transect agreeing with the first two stops nothing. The archive is cheap and genuinely informative, and it still does not decide noon.
assumes: evidence is worth what it changes, not what it costs
a second measurement of the same kind narrows the same thing again
answerText: Lower the monitor into the gallery. It is the only measurement taken where the crew will be, and it is the only one whose result changes whether they go in.

title: A cause, and a coincidence that looks like one
task: Make the tone follow one machine
scene: A new tone appeared on the array overnight at 214 hertz. Four machines changed state in the same hour. Achterberg has the plant log and the sonar operator is waiting.
question: Four candidates, one tone. Establish which machine is producing it and prove it.
takeaway: A relationship is causal when it reverses, not when it coincides.
why: Four things changed in one hour, so the log alone cannot name a cause; it can only name candidates. Securing several at once makes the display quieter and settles nothing, because a quieter display is consistent with any of them being responsible. One variable at a time gives a candidate, and restoring it is what turns the candidate into a cause: a coincidence does not come back on demand. The reversal also costs almost nothing here, which is worth noticing — the reason it gets skipped is not expense, it is that by then the answer already feels known.
assumes: a controlled test changes one variable and holds the rest
a machinery-order tone scales with the rate of the machine producing it
answerText: Seawater pump B. Securing it alone drops the tone nineteen decibels, and restoring it brings the line straight back — which is what separates it from the machine that happened to start in the same hour.

title: Any size you like, for the right albedo
task: Get a size out of a brightness
scene: One brightness measurement, and a model with two knobs in it. Kit Sorensen has the thermal data on a second screen and has not brought it over yet.
question: Match the brightness, then say what size it is.
takeaway: One observable across two unknowns fixes a family of solutions, not a solution.
why: The brightness is the product of an area and a reflectivity, so halving one and quadrupling the other reproduces it exactly. That is not a noisy measurement; it is a measurement of one number where two are wanted, and a better telescope slides along the same curve. Thermal infrared breaks it because it responds to the absorbed fraction rather than the reflected one — the same albedo that makes an object faint makes it warm — so its curve runs the other way and the two cross once. What comes out is a diameter. The density underneath it is still an assumption wearing a number.
assumes: reflected brightness depends on the product of area and reflectivity
absorbed and reflected fractions of the incident light sum to one
answerText: About 180 metres, at a reflectivity near 0.14 — and that is the diameter measured, not the density or the strength, which are still inferred from a surface classification.

title: The small anchor and the large panel
task: Follow the force to the ground
scene: The gym is cleared on a rapid inspection. Naidoo has the drawings out and the roof-to-panel anchors are the only thing on them with no capacity written beside it.
question: Put the transfers in the order the force takes, then name the one that decides whether the path holds.
takeaway: A load path is governed by its weakest required transfer, whatever the elements either side of it can carry.
why: Force does not travel from a roof to the ground by being near it. Every interface has to carry what the one above it delivers, and the path is limited by whichever required transfer is weakest — which has nothing to do with the size of the elements on either side. The panel is the largest thing here by a wide margin and it is not the question; if the anchor cannot pass the roof and wall inertia across the joint, the panel's own strength has nothing to act against and a heavy element is left unsupported out of plane. That is why the item with no number beside it is the item to test.
assumes: lateral force reaches the ground through a continuous set of physical connections
a chain of transfers is limited by the weakest one the path requires
answerText: Roof deck, collector, roof-to-panel anchor, wall panel, foundation — governed by the anchor, the one transfer in the path with no tested capacity behind it.

title: What twenty bottles cannot ask
task: Spend twenty slots on a plan you can defend
scene: A crate with twenty laboratory slots in it, the river map on the wall, and the partition model's prediction pinned beside it. Nobody has written down a recommended plan.
question: Twenty slots. Build the plan, and know which of the four questions it leaves open.
takeaway: Sampling is experimental design under a budget, and every feasible plan forgoes a question.
why: Every line on this crate is worth sampling, which is exactly why a list of options cannot teach the decision: read one at a time they are all justified. A finite inventory makes the trade concrete — the sediment cores and the second time point together cost more than what is left after the protected slots, so a plan that asks whether the concentration is rising cannot also ask whether there is a reservoir underneath it. The error worth avoiding is not choosing badly. It is finishing the programme without having noticed that a question was silently dropped, and reporting reassurance built on the phase nobody sampled.
assumes: a contaminant divides between water, suspended particles and sediment
a measurement without a blank cannot be defended afterwards
answerText: Any plan that keeps the intake and the QC and stays inside twenty slots is defensible — and it will answer two of the remaining three questions at most. Naming which one you left open is the answer.

title: Three circles and an area
task: Report where it was, not how far
scene: Three stations, three arrival separations, and a regional map. The ridge station's clock has been drifting since the spring and there is a correction sheet for it on the bench.
question: Switch the stations in, decide what to do about the ridge clock, and report the position.
takeaway: One station gives a distance, three give a region, and a timing error moves the whole region.
why: One station's arrival separation says how far the source was. It says nothing about direction, so on its own it leaves a whole ring. Three rings intersect, and what they intersect in is an area, not a point. Reporting a coordinate claims a precision the arrival times do not support, and somebody downstream will treat it as certain. The clock matters because the calculation runs on times, not on waveforms. A station biased by six tenths of a second draws its ring in the wrong place. Its own record looks perfectly normal, and the intersection moves with it.
assumes: two wave types travelling at different speeds separate further with distance
a location computed from arrival times inherits any error in those times
answerText: Around 24 east, 24 north, as a region several kilometres across — and only after the ridge clock correction, which moves that station's ring fourteen kilometres.

title: Moving the dot and moving the cloud
task: Get the distribution inside the corridor
scene: The corridor runs 5.3 to 7.7 degrees. The current solution sits at 6.9 with nine tenths of a degree on it, and a fifth of the trajectories are outside.
question: Bring the entry solution inside the corridor, and say when it is ready.
takeaway: Re-centring moves the whole distribution; only new information makes it narrower.
why: The nominal angle is the one place the vehicle is least likely to be. Re-targeting it slides the whole distribution across without changing its width. The fraction outside the corridor barely moves; the trajectories that were long become shallow instead. What is being asked is not where to aim but how much the measurements permit, and only new tracking reduces that. It costs hours the day would rather spend elsewhere. That is the real decision, because the corridor is a survivability limit and does not negotiate.
assumes: a state estimate is a distribution over what the measurements permit
the limits of a corridor come from survivability, not from navigation
answerText: Both tracking passes. Re-centring alone leaves better than one trajectory in twenty outside the corridor; narrowing the spread is the only thing that moves that number.

title: A confirmed impact is not a confirmed deflection
task: Find out what the impact actually did
scene: The impactor arrived on Tuesday and the confirmation is on the wall. The ejecta enhancement was quoted as somewhere between one and five. Three tracking passes remain in the budget.
question: Predict the period change, commit the impact, and report what happened.
takeaway: An intervention is verified by measuring what it changed, not by confirming that it happened.
why: The spacecraft's own momentum is known to a few percent. What is not known is how much more the ejecta carried away, and quoting that as a single number rather than the factor of several it actually is turns an honest uncertainty into a false prediction. Both halves of the error are ordinary; the failure that is specific to this decision is finishing without measuring. Confirmation of impact is confirmation of an event, not of an effect, and if the tracking budget goes on refining the pre-impact orbit there is nothing left to compare it against — the campaign then produces a photograph instead of a result.
assumes: momentum leaving a surface as ejecta carries some of the transferred impulse
an orbital period change is measurable by tracking
answerText: Around fourteen and a half minutes — but only the post-impact tracking establishes it. A confirmed impact with no measured orbit is a confirmed impact and nothing else.

title: Rules, and the lead time they need
task: Write the thresholds before tonight's update
scene: The response board is blank. The current probability is one in two and a half thousand, the next update lands tonight, and Calderón wants the board signed before it does.
question: Set each stage's threshold, release the board, and stand by what it does.
takeaway: A rule written before the data is a decision; the same rule written afterwards is a reaction.
why: Two ways of getting this wrong look nothing alike and cost the same. A threshold set too high never fires, and the stage simply does not happen. A threshold set at a sensible number fires on the day nine update with three hundred hours left, which is a correct rule for an action that needed three hundred and thirty-six — so the rule is satisfied and the evacuation is already impossible. The day fifteen collapse to one in nine thousand does not make the day nine decision a mistake, and the board is what makes that arguable afterwards, because it was signed before anybody knew.
assumes: a probability is a statement about knowledge rather than about the object
a staged response has a lead time that cannot be compressed
answerText: Every threshold has to sit low enough to fire while its own lead time is still available — the evacuation stage below about 0.3 per cent, since it needs fourteen days and only the first two updates arrive with that much left.

dayTitle: Which number is carrying the error
title: The exponent is not the whole story
task: Decide which measurement is worth buying
scene: The energy figure is on the board to three significant figures. Merrick has the three inputs it was built from beside it, each with what it is actually known to, and one measurement slot left in the day.
question: One measurement is affordable. Which of these is carrying the uncertainty in the energy?
takeaway: A term's contribution is its own width times its exponent, so a badly known number with no power over it can dominate a well-known one cubed.
why: A term contributes its exponent multiplied by its own fractional width. The radius is cubed, which is the part everybody sees, and it is known well enough that three times eight per cent is still smaller than one times forty-five. Buying another radar pass therefore improves the number that was already good and moves the total almost not at all. What makes this worth catching is that the shortcut — rank by exponent — is reasonable, teachable and produces exactly the wrong answer here. The density is also the term nobody can measure directly from orbit, which is why it stays wide.
assumes: fractional uncertainties combine weighted by the power each term is raised to
a measured quantity and an inferred one are different kinds of number
answerText: The density. It is raised to the first power and known to forty-five per cent, which outweighs a radius cubed and known to eight — so the sampling is the measurement worth buying, and the energy is a range rather than a figure.

dayTitle: Which number is carrying the error
title: Best at the nominal, and nowhere else
task: Choose the option that survives the assumption moving
scene: Four remediation options are ranked on the board, all at one figure for how long the containment holds. Tomas Oyelaran has the range that figure actually came with and has said nothing about it.
question: Move the endurance through its range, then choose the option you would commit to.
takeaway: A choice that is only best at the nominal is a choice that has not been tested.
why: At seventy-eight hours the direct excavation finishes first and looks like the obvious call. The endurance was never seventy-eight hours; it was a range with seventy-eight in the middle of it, and at the low end the direct option needs more containment than there is. What the slider shows is that three of the four options are conditional on an assumption holding, and the ranking everybody was reading is a ranking of what happens if it does. Choosing the staged option costs thirteen hours and buys the property that the plan does not have to be abandoned partway.
assumes: an assumption stated as a range is not a value
an option is only available while the conditions it needs still hold
answerText: The staged excavation. It is not the fastest at the nominal and it is the only one still possible at the pessimistic end of the endurance range, which is the end nobody measured away.

dayTitle: Which number is carrying the error
title: A pattern is not an outlier
task: Say which fit you would propagate
scene: Three fits of the same subsidence survey are on Priya Naidoo's screen, within two hundredths of a millimetre of each other on the summary statistic. The residuals are plotted where each marker actually sits.
question: Look at each field before you choose. Which of these fits would you propagate forward?
takeaway: A low summary statistic with a pattern under it hides a systematic that will bias every later prediction the same way.
why: Two of these three leave residuals that are positive on one side of the site and negative on the other. That is not scatter; it is a quantity the model does not contain, and adding a free parameter that soaks it up improves the summary statistic while leaving the cause in place. It will then bias every extrapolation in the same direction, quietly, because nothing about the fit looks wrong afterwards. The re-levelled fit scores worse and its residuals change sign at random, which is what a complete model produces. One large residual would be a bad marker; six small ones in a pattern are a cause.
assumes: a complete model leaves residuals that look like noise
a fitted parameter can absorb a systematic without removing it
answerText: The re-levelled fit, at 0.19. The tilt term scores better and its residuals still change sign across the site, which means it absorbed the benchmark error into a parameter rather than removing it.

title: The loudest is not the first
task: Take one condition and hand over the rest
scene: Four conditions, one watch team, and a clock that runs whether or not anybody has decided. Ruth Calderón will take whichever one you leave her, and she wants the others owned.
question: Which do you change first, and who has the others?
takeaway: A handover is an owner, a first action and a condition that brings them back; two of the three is nobody watching it.
why: The fire panel is the loudest thing in the building and it has been stable for twenty minutes on a fault that is already in the log. The spill is rising and it is inside a bund, so what it costs is money and time rather than an option. The groundwater is the only condition where waiting removes a choice: over the sill, the records are gone and no amount of later effort brings them back. That is what puts it first — not the rate, not the noise, but a margin closing on something irreversible. Everything else can be somebody else's if they are told when to come back.
assumes: a trend and a rate say more than a current value
an instruction without a return condition produces no report until it is too late
answerText: Take the groundwater yourself. It is the only one whose margin is closing on something that cannot be undone, and everything else goes out with an owner, a first action and a condition that brings them back.

title: You stopped driving. You did not stop
task: Stop the trolley where you meant to
scene: The survey trolley runs on a rail in the flooded gallery, where nothing slows it down. Ben Achterberg has the last operator's trace, which shows the motor cut at the mark and the trolley eighteen metres past it.
question: Set the pulse and the distance at which braking starts, then run it and see where it stops.
takeaway: With nothing to damp it, the braking impulse has to begin before the target, by exactly as far as the acceleration carried it.
why: The trolley leaves the acceleration with a speed, and on a rail in still water there is nothing to take that speed away except an equal impulse in the other direction. So the braking has to start early, and by a specific amount: the distance covered while the brake is working, which is set by the same pulse that produced the speed. Cutting the drive at the mark is not braking at all — it only stops adding speed, and the trolley carries the speed it already has. A longer pulse gets there sooner and needs a longer brake and more of the budget, which is the trade the two controls actually make.
assumes: a body with no resisting force keeps whatever velocity it was given
removing a velocity takes the same impulse that produced it
answerText: Braking has to start about seven and a half metres short of the mark on a six-second pulse — around 82 metres — because that is how far the trolley travels while the braking impulse is being applied.

title: More detections, the same amount of notice
task: Find what the network cannot see
scene: Five thousand synthetic events with known times and sizes, ready to push through the monitoring network exactly as a real one would go. Kit Sorensen has the recovery display up and nothing on it yet.
question: Run the configurations you want, then fund the upgrade that actually buys something.
takeaway: Injecting a population whose truth you know measures the pipeline rather than the world, and what never comes back is not absent.
why: Lowering the threshold more than doubles the count, which is the number everybody reports, and it adds two hours of notice. What the injection shows is that the extra events are ones the network was already going to catch, only slightly earlier. The direction above the divide produces no recoveries in any configuration at all, and that is not a property of the events — the truth is known and they are there. It is a property of where the stations are. A discovery is worth what the downstream response can do with the time it buys, so a configuration that finds more and warns no earlier has bought a longer list.
assumes: a detection pipeline has a selection function, and it can be measured
a warning is only useful if it arrives while something can still be done
answerText: The upstream stations. They recover the fewest additional events of any upgrade and more than triple the median warning time, because they are the only ones that see the direction the network is currently blind to.

title: Where you are, and how you know
task: Learn the route, then find it again
scene: The lower vault runs as one line of rooms with a door at each end. Priya Naidoo walks it with you once with the labels up, and mentions that one of the doors sticks.
question: Walk it lit, then put it back together in the dark — and say where you are when the route is broken.
takeaway: A sequence of recognisable places can be re-entered at any point; a count of anything cannot.
why: A pace count and a turn count both produce an answer and neither can be resumed. Once the route is broken the count is measuring a journey that did not happen, and there is no way to check it from inside the building. A sequence of places has the property the count does not: every element of it is recognisable on its own, so being put down in the middle of it is recoverable. Naming where you are is the whole of the recovery, and it is only possible because each room has something in it that no other room has.
assumes: a count of paces or turns cannot be resumed once it is interrupted
a place can be recognised from something in it that is not a label
answerText: Deed store, map room, microfilm bay, bindery, transfer room, strong room — and after the jammed door you are in the transfer room, because the trolley ramp is only in one of them.

title: What can be signed off
task: Say what the fortnight established
scene: Ruth Calderón has the fortnight's findings on one sheet and a transfer on Friday. She wants to know which of them she is entitled to put her name to.
question: Which of these can the office state without qualification?
takeaway: What a verification office establishes is bounded by what it actually measured.
why: The office measured a reference factor and recomputed the ratios that used it. That is a bounded claim with a stated basis, and it is the only one on this list. The second is the same number stretched into a frequency range nobody worked in. The third inverts what was found — the gauge was the independent instrument and it stands. The fourth throws away the correctly measured numerators along with the mislabelled denominator, which is the failure the whole fortnight was about.
assumes: a corrected ratio and an uncorrected one are different claims

choices: The Halden site ratio is 4.8 against competent rock, corrected for the vault reference.
The Halden site amplifies ground motion by a factor of five at all frequencies.
The mechanical gauge reading was wrong and has been discarded.
Every measurement taken at Halden this fortnight is unreliable.
rebuttals: The correction was made in one frequency band, and the ratio outside it was never measured.
The gauge is the channel that did not use the vault, so it is the one thing untouched by the error.
The numerators were measured correctly; only the label on the denominator was wrong.

title: What each claim is standing on
task: Match each finding to the evidence it actually rests on.
scene: Four findings from the fortnight, and four different kinds of evidence underneath them. Tomas Oyelaran wants them paired before anything is filed.
takeaway: A claim is only as strong as the kind of evidence under it, and the two are easy to swap.
why: Each of these findings is strong, and each is strong for a different reason. Confusing them is how a bounded claim turns into a general one somewhere downstream.
assumes: different kinds of evidence support different kinds of claim

choices: A rate measured directly, plus a removal term that was running throughout.
A single variable changed and then restored, with the feature following it both ways.
Two measurements responding to the same property through different physics.
An inspection that found the physical condition did not match the record.
scenarios: The inflow at the hull was 410 litres a minute.
The tone at 214 hertz came from seawater pump B.
The asteroid is about 180 metres across.
The aft escape route could not be signed off.

title: What the gate is doing to the river
task: Turn a gate opening into a rate of discharge
scene: The gate is winding open at a steady rate and the head above the sill is 2.0 metres. Ada Merrick needs the discharge rate written down before the shift changes, and the gauge downstream only reports what has already arrived.
question: Derive how fast the discharge is rising, in terms of how fast the head is rising.
takeaway: A rate on the left needs every factor the right-hand side's own change brings with it.
why: The discharge does not follow the gate; it follows the head, and it follows it through a three-halves power. That exponent is why a spillway is hard to run: the same half metre of head does far more when the head is already high, so a rate that looked manageable an hour ago is not the rate you have now. The chain rule is what carries the head's own motion into the discharge, and dropping its inner factor leaves you with dQ/dH — a slope that is perfectly correct about a question nobody asked.
assumes: the discharge over a weir depends on the head raised to a power
a quantity that changes because another one changes needs the chain rule
answerText: dQ/dt ≈ 44.5·dH/dt — so a head rising at 0.05 m/min raises the discharge by about 2.2 cubic metres a second every minute.
